criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

A 28-yr-old man comes to the outpatient clinic for evaluation of a lump in his right testis. About 1
month ago, while taking a shower, he noted a hard area in his right testis that felt "like a
marble." He had never noticed this before and decided to wait and see if anything would
change. When the mass did not go away, he scheduled this appointment. Today, he states the
lump is not painful or tender to the touch and has not changed in size. He has had annual
physical exams and was never told that a lump was present. Four years ago, he had a scrotal
ultrasound following a brief episode of scrotal discomfort after competing in a bicycle race; the
result of the ultrasound was normal.

Review of Systems:
General: Overall feels well. Denies any weight loss, fevers, or chills.

Skin: Denies rashes, itching, or other lesions.

HEENT: Noncontributory

Pulmonary: No cough or shortness of breath.

Cardiovascular: No palpitations or chest pain.

Gastrointestinal: Good appetite, bowel movements are normal. Denies nausea or vomiting.
Denies abdominal or flank pain.

Genitourinary: No dysuria, hematuria, frequency, or urgency. No urethral discharge.

Musculoskeletal: No back or joint pain, no leg swelling.

Neurologic: Noncontributory

Psychiatric: Noncontributory

Past Medical History:
Medical history: No reported medical history. Denies history of urinary tract infections, difficulty
with urination, immunosuppressive disorders, or sexually transmitted infections.

Surgical history: Rotator cuff repair 4 yr ago; left inguinal hernia repair as a child.

Medications: Occasional NSAIDs.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

Family history: Mother and father healthy. No history of genitourinary malignancies in any
known relatives.

Social history: He denies current or previous tobacco use. He exercises almost every day with a
combination of weight training and cardio. He works primarily at a desk job with somewhat
frequent travel. All relevant immunizations are up to date. He denies exposure to any sick
contacts. He has had unprotected sex only with his wife for the past 3 yr.

Physical Examination:
General appearance: Thin male who appears fatigued and older than stated age; in no apparent
respiratory distress.

Vital signs:
Temperature: 37° C
Pulse: 60 beats/min
BP: 112/65 mm Hg
Respirations: 16/min
Height: 6'
Weight: 180 lb
BMI: 24.4

Skin: Warm and dry to the touch.

HEENT: Nasopharynx appears normal; no neck masses or lymphadenopathy.

Pulmonary: Breath sounds present and equal bilaterally. No stridor, rales, or wheezing.

Cardiovascular: Heart rate is regular; radial and dorsalis pedis pulses are present and equal
bilaterally; no pedal edema.

Gastrointestinal: Abdomen is not distended; there are no ecchymoses. Normal bowel sounds
are present. Abdomen is soft and nontender to light and deep palpation; no masses are present.

Genitourinary: Circumcised phallus, no visible lesions, bilateral descended testes. Left testis
smooth and nontender. Left epididymis is normal in texture and nontender. Right testis has firm
mass in the midsection that is nontender on palpation. Right epididymis is normal in texture and
nontender. There are no palpable inguinal lymph nodes. No urethral discharge.

Musculoskeletal: No costovertebral angle tenderness.

Neurologic: Unremarkable

Mental status: Alert and oriented to person, place, and time.

Age: 28  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Right testicular lump (hard, non‑tender, present for ~1 month)  

Analysis: The patient presents with a firm, non‑tender intratesticular mass on the right side. Physical examination confirms a solid‑appearing lesion without pain, epididymal involvement, or inguinal lymphadenopathy. In a young adult male, a solid intratesticular mass is highly suspicious for a testicular germ‑cell tumor. Differential considerations include benign entities (e.g., epididymal cyst, hydrocele, varicocele, infection/abscess) but these are typically cystic or extra‑testicular and often painful. The scrotal ultrasound (provided) is interpreted as a **solid testicular mass**, supporting the malignant suspicion. No systemic symptoms are reported, and there is no family history of GU malignancy.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Serum tumor markers (alpha‑fetoprotein, beta‑human chorionic gonadotropin, lactate dehydrogenase); referral for scrotal ultrasound review if needed; consider staging CT (chest/abdomen/pelvis) after definitive diagnosis.

Conclusion: The findings are most consistent with a solid testicular neoplasm, likely a germ‑cell tumor, requiring prompt urologic evaluation and work‑up.

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  

Subclinical specialization: Urology  

Recommendations:  
1. Order serum tumor markers (AFP, β‑hCG, LDH) promptly.  
2. Refer the patient to a urologist for definitive management—typically radical inguinal orchiectomy within 1–2 weeks.  
3. Discuss fertility preservation (semen banking) before surgery, given potential impact on spermatogenesis.  
4. Counsel on testicular self‑examination and educate regarding signs of recurrence.  
5. After orchiectomy and pathology, proceed with appropriate staging imaging (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis) and multidisciplinary oncology referral as indicated.  

Notes: None

Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.

criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

Vignette:
A 7-year-old girl presents with abrupt onset of fever, nausea, vomiting, and sore throat. The child denies cough, rhinorrhea, or nasal congestion. On physical exam, oral temperature is 101°F (38.5°C) and there is an exudative pharyngitis, with enlarged cervical lymph nodes. A rapid antigen test is positive for group A Streptococcus (GAS).
winner_protocol:
Age: 7 years  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Abrupt onset fever, nausea, vomiting, and sore throat with exudative pharyngitis and cervical lymphadenopathy.  
Analysis: The child presents with classic signs of acute streptococcal pharyngitis (fever, exudative tonsils, tender cervical nodes) and a positive rapid antigen test for group A Streptococcus, confirming the diagnosis. Differential considerations include viral pharyngitis, infectious mononucleosis, and peritonsillar cellulitis; however, the lack of cough, rhinorrhea, and the positive GAS test make bacterial streptococcal infection the most likely. No signs of airway compromise or severe systemic illness are present.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  
Conclusion: Acute group A Streptococcus pharyngitis in a 7‑year‑old girl.  
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics  
Recommendations:  
- Initiate antibiotic therapy: Penicillin V 250 mg PO twice daily (or amoxicillin 50 mg/kg/day divided BID) for 10 days.  
- Provide symptomatic care: antipyretics (acetaminophen or ibuprofen), adequate oral hydration, and anti‑emetics if vomiting persists.  
- Advise the family on infection control (hand hygiene, avoid sharing utensils) and to keep the child home from school until 24 hours after antibiotics have been started and fever resolved.  
- Counsel regarding signs of complications (e.g., worsening throat pain, drooling, difficulty breathing, rash, joint pain) that would warrant prompt reevaluation.  
- Schedule a follow‑up visit in 48–72 hours or sooner if symptoms worsen.  
Notes: None

Diagnosis10cm: Thyrotoxicosis with diffuse goiter with thyrotoxic crisis or storm
Vignette: A 32-year-old woman with a history of Graves disease (non-compliant with methimazole for 2 months) presents with 2 days of palpitations, agitation, profuse sweating, and diarrhea. She had a dental extraction 3 days ago. On examination, she is markedly agitated, tremulous, and unable to remain still. Vital signs: T 40.0C (104F), HR 162 (atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response), RR 28, BP 168/60 (widened pulse pressure), SpO2 97%. She has a fine tremor, bilateral proptosis, lid lag, diffuse goiter with an audible bruit, and brisk reflexes throughout. Skin is warm and moist. She becomes increasingly confused during the examination. Labs: TSH <0.01 mIU/L, free T4 7.8 ng/dL (normal 0.8-1.8), free T3 22 pg/mL (normal 2.3-4.2). Burch-Wartofsky score is 65 (highly suggestive of thyroid storm). Propranolol, PTU, hydrocortisone, and iodine solution are initiated.

Vignette:
A 32-year-old woman with a history of Graves disease (non-compliant with methimazole for 2 months) presents with 2 days of palpitations, agitation, profuse sweating, and diarrhea. She had a dental extraction 3 days ago. On examination, she is markedly agitated, tremulous, and unable to remain still. Vital signs: T 40.0C (104F), HR 162 (atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response), RR 28, BP 168/60 (widened pulse pressure), SpO2 97%. She has a fine tremor, bilateral proptosis, lid lag, diffuse goiter with an audible bruit, and brisk reflexes throughout. Skin is warm and moist. She becomes increasingly confused during the examination. Labs: TSH <0.01 mIU/L, free T4 7.8 ng/dL (normal 0.8-1.8), free T3 22 pg/mL (normal 2.3-4.2). Burch-Wartofsky score is 65 (highly suggestive of thyroid storm). Propranolol, PTU, hydrocortisone, and iodine solution are initiated.

Age: 32  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Acute onset of palpitations, agitation, profuse sweating, diarrhea, high fever, and progressive confusion in a known Graves disease patient non‑compliant with antithyroid therapy.  

Analysis: The patient presents with classic features of thyroid storm: severe hyperthermia (40 °C), tachyarrhythmia (atrial fibrillation with HR 162), widened pulse pressure, tremor, hyperreflexia, diaphoresis, gastrointestinal hypermotility, and altered mental status. Laboratory data confirm extreme thyrotoxicosis (TSH < 0.01 mIU/L, free T4 7.8 ng/dL, free T3 22 pg/mL) and the Burch‑Wartofsky score of 65 is highly predictive. Precipitating factor is recent dental extraction. Differential considerations (sepsis, pheochromocytoma, drug intoxication) are less likely given the thyroid panel and clinical picture, but infection must still be excluded because it can coexist and further worsen the storm.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests:  
- 12‑lead ECG (already shows atrial fibrillation) and continuous cardiac telemetry  
- Serum electrolytes, renal function, liver function tests, and glucose  
- Complete blood count with differential  
- Blood cultures (to rule out concurrent infection)  
- Chest radiograph (baseline for possible pulmonary complications)  
- Thyroid antibody panel (optional, not urgent)  

Conclusion: The patient is experiencing a life‑threatening thyroid storm precipitated by untreated Graves disease and recent dental surgery, with hemodynamic instability and atrial fibrillation requiring immediate intensive management.  

Emergency type: Requires emergent care  

Subclinical specialization: Endocrinology  

Recommendations:  
1. **Intensive Care Unit admission** for close hemodynamic, cardiac, and neurologic monitoring.  
2. **Continue and optimize antithyroid therapy**:  
   - Propylthiouracil (PTU) 500 mg PO/NG loading dose, then 250 mg q6h (adjust for liver function).  
   - Iodine solution (e.g., Lugol’s iodine) 1 g PO/NG q8h, initiated ≥1 hour after PTU.  
3. **Beta‑blockade**: Propranolol 60–80 mg PO/NG q6h (or IV esmolol infusion if oral not tolerated) to control tachycardia and reduce peripheral conversion of T4 → T3.  
4. **Glucocorticoids**: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV q8h to inhibit T4‑to‑T3 conversion and address possible relative adrenal insufficiency.  
5. **Supportive measures**:  
   - Aggressive cooling (evaporative, antipyretics).  
   - Intravenous isotonic fluids with electrolyte replacement; monitor for hypokalemia (especially if beta‑blocker used).  
   - Oxygen supplementation to maintain SpO₂ > 94 %.  
   - Continuous cardiac monitoring; consider rate‑control agents (e.g., diltiazem) if beta‑blocker contraindicated.  
6. **Treat atrial fibrillation**: Rate control with propranolol; anticoagulation assessment after stabilization (CHA₂DS₂‑VASc low in this age, but consider if prolonged).  
7. **Infection work‑up**: Obtain blood cultures, CBC, and chest X‑ray; start empiric broad‑spectrum antibiotics only if clinical suspicion of infection arises.  
8. **Monitor for complications**: Hepatotoxicity from PTU, worsening heart failure, pulmonary edema, and neurologic deterioration.  
9. **Re‑evaluate thyroid function** after 24–48 h to gauge response; adjust PTU dosing accordingly.  
10. **Patient education** (post‑recovery): Importance of strict adherence to antithyroid medication, regular endocrinology follow‑up, and avoidance of precipitating stressors.  

Notes: None.

Vignette:
A 70-year-old man with a history of chronic HTN and atrial fibrillation is witnessed by a family member to have nausea, vomiting, and right-sided weakness, as well as difficulty speaking and comprehending language. The symptoms started with only mild slurred speech before progressing over several minutes to severe aphasia and right arm paralysis. The patient is taking warfarin.
winner_protocol:
Age: 70  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Sudden onset nausea, vomiting, right‑sided weakness and severe aphasia with difficulty speaking and understanding, progressing over minutes.  
Analysis: The rapid evolution of focal neurological deficits (right arm paralysis, expressive and receptive aphasia) in a patient with atrial fibrillation on warfarin strongly suggests an acute left middle cerebral artery (MCA) ischemic stroke, most likely cardio‑embolic. Critical considerations include:  
- Intracerebral hemorrhage (must be excluded before thrombolysis).  
- Warfarin anticoagulation status (INR may be therapeutic, sub‑therapeutic, or supratherapeutic).  
- Other mimics (hypoglycemia, seizure with post‑ictal paresis) are less likely given the pattern and progression.  
The priority is rapid neuro‑imaging and laboratory assessment to determine eligibility for reperfusion therapy and to guide anticoagulation reversal if needed.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Non‑contrast head CT (emergency), CT angiography of head/neck (if available), INR (and full coagulation panel), basic metabolic panel, CBC, point‑of‑care glucose, NIH Stroke Scale assessment.  
Conclusion: Acute left hemispheric ischemic stroke, likely cardio‑embolic, requiring immediate emergent evaluation and possible reperfusion therapy.  
Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Neurology  
Recommendations:  
1. Activate stroke code immediately.  
2. Perform rapid bedside NIHSS and obtain vital signs.  
3. Obtain point‑of‑care glucose to rule out hypoglycemia.  
4. Draw blood for INR, CBC, BMP; expedite results.  
5. Obtain non‑contrast head CT within 10 minutes of arrival; add CT‑angiography if large‑vessel occlusion is suspected and the facility can perform endovascular therapy.  
6. If CT shows no hemorrhage and symptom onset is ≤4.5 hours with INR ≤1.7, consider IV alteplase per guidelines.  
7. If large‑vessel occlusion is identified and patient meets criteria, arrange for endovascular thrombectomy (≤6 hours, up to 24 hours in select cases).  
8. If INR is supratherapeutic or hemorrhage is identified, reverse warfarin with vitamin K ± 4‑factor prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) per protocol.  
9. Manage blood pressure according to stroke guidelines (maintain SBP <185 mm Hg for tPA eligibility).  
10. Provide supportive care: airway protection, anti‑emetics, monitor for neurological deterioration.  
Notes: None.

Vignette:
A 25-year-old woman presents with a 4-day history of an itchy red rash on both wrists. She recently purchased a new costume jewelry bracelet and has been wearing it daily. She denies any blistering, weeping, or spreading of the rash beyond the areas of contact. She has no history of eczema or other skin conditions. On examination, there are well-demarcated erythematous patches on both wrists corresponding to where the bracelet sits. There is mild scaling but no vesiculation, excoriation, or secondary infection. The remainder of the skin exam is normal.

Age: 25  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Itchy red rash on both wrists associated with daily wear of a new costume‑jewelry bracelet.  
Analysis: The rash is confined to the areas of contact with the bracelet, is well‑demarcated, erythematous with mild scaling, and lacks vesiculation, weeping, or secondary infection. The temporal relationship (4 days after starting the bracelet) and absence of prior skin disease strongly suggest allergic contact dermatitis, most commonly due to nickel or other metal allergens in costume jewelry. Differential considerations such as irritant contact dermatitis, early infection, or a primary dermatosis (e.g., eczema, psoriasis) are less likely given the lack of spreading, no vesicles, and normal skin elsewhere.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  
Conclusion: Allergic contact dermatitis secondary to the new costume jewelry bracelet.  
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate  
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology  
Recommendations:  
1. Immediately discontinue wearing the bracelet (and any other suspected metal accessories).  
2. Apply a low‑potency topical corticosteroid (e.g., hydrocortisone 1 % cream) to the affected wrists twice daily for up to 7 days.  
3. Use a fragrance‑free emollient or moisturizer to restore barrier function.  
4. Consider an oral antihistamine (e.g., cetirizine 10 mg daily) for pruritus if needed.  
5. Keep the area clean and dry; avoid scratching to prevent secondary infection.  
6. Re‑evaluate in 5‑7 days; if no improvement or if signs of infection develop (increased warmth, pain, purulent drainage), seek non‑emergent medical care.  
7. If rash recurs with other metal exposures, arrange for patch testing with a dermatologist to identify specific allergens.  
Notes: None.

winner_protocol:
Age: 28  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Small, painful fluid‑filled vesicles on the left lower lip with a preceding tingling/burning sensation.  
Analysis: The presentation is classic for recurrent herpes labialis (HSV‑1 reactivation). Supporting facts include: prodromal tingling, clustered vesicles on an erythematous base at the vermilion border, recurrence approximately twice yearly for 5 years, and absence of systemic signs or intra‑oral lesions. Main differentials to consider are: aphthous ulcer (usually ulcerative, not vesicular), contact dermatitis (usually non‑vesicular or with a clear irritant exposure), and impetigo (honey‑colored crusts, not preceded by tingling). The recurrent pattern, prodrome, and lesion morphology strongly favor HSV‑1.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  
Conclusion: Recurrent herpes labialis (cold sore) due to HSV‑1 reactivation.  
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology  
Recommendations:  
1. Initiate antiviral therapy promptly (within 72 h of symptom onset):  
   • Topical acyclovir 5% ointment five times daily for 5 days **or**  
   • Oral antiviral (acyclovir 400 mg five times daily, valacyclovir 1 g twice daily, or famciclovir 500 mg twice daily) for 1 day if lesions are extensive, painful, or patient prefers systemic therapy.  
2. Provide symptomatic relief: lip balm with sunscreen, cool compresses, analgesic (e.g., ibuprofen or acetaminophen).  
3. Counsel on trigger avoidance: stress management, adequate sleep, sun protection on lips, and avoidance of lip licking.  
4. Advise against touching or picking lesions; wash hands frequently to prevent autoinoculation.  
5. Discuss transmission precautions: avoid kissing, oral sex, and sharing utensils while lesions are present.  
6. If episodes exceed 4 per year or are particularly severe, consider prophylactic oral antiviral (e.g., valacyclovir 500 mg daily).  
7. Follow‑up in 1–2 weeks if lesions do not improve, worsen, or develop secondary bacterial infection; consider viral PCR or culture only if atypical.  
Notes: None

Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.

Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.

criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

winner_protocol:
Age: 50  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Acute worsening lower back pain radiating to both legs with bilateral leg weakness, urinary retention, and perianal sensory loss.  
Analysis: The patient presents with classic signs of cauda equina syndrome (CES): severe back pain, bilateral lower‑extremity motor weakness (3/5), loss of ankle reflexes, diminished perianal sensation, reduced anal sphincter tone, and a post‑void residual of 650 mL. MRI confirms a large central L4‑L5 disc herniation compressing the cauda equina nerve roots, which is the most likely etiology. Differential considerations such as spinal epidural abscess, metastatic tumor, or severe spinal stenosis are less likely given the acute presentation, lack of systemic signs, and clear disc pathology on imaging.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  
Conclusion: Cauda equina syndrome secondary to a large central L4‑L5 disc herniation.  
Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Orthopedics  
Recommendations:  
1. Immediate urinary catheterization to decompress bladder and monitor output.  
2. Urgent consultation with spine surgery (orthopedic or neurosurgical) for emergent decompressive surgery (e.g., L4‑L5 laminectomy and discectomy) ideally within 24 hours.  
3. Initiate high‑dose intravenous corticosteroids only if surgical delay is anticipated and no contraindications exist.  
4. Provide analgesia and consider neuromuscular blockade monitoring; keep the patient NPO pending surgery.  
5. Admit to a monitored unit; serial neurologic examinations every 2–4 hours.  
6. Post‑operative plan includes early mobilization, physical therapy, and bladder function reassessment.  
Notes: None

winner_protocol:
Age: 25  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Bilateral thigh soreness beginning 36 hours after first gym session with squats and lunges, worsened by movement (e.g., descending stairs).  

Analysis: The temporal relationship (pain onset ~24‑48 h after unaccustomed eccentric exercise) and bilateral, symmetric involvement of quadriceps and hamstrings are classic for delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS). Supporting facts include mild tenderness without edema, ecchymosis, warmth, joint effusion, or loss of range of motion, and the absence of acute injury, popping sensation, or systemic symptoms. Main differentials such as strain/tear, rhabdomyolysis, infection, inflammatory arthritis, or myopathy are less likely given the lack of focal deficits, swelling, systemic signs, and normal examination.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  

Conclusion: The presentation is most consistent with delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS) secondary to novel eccentric lower‑extremity exercise.  

Emergency type: Self-care appropriate  

Subclinical specialization: Orthopedics  

Recommendations:  
1. Reassure the patient that DOMS is a benign, self‑limited condition.  
2. Advise activity modification: avoid high‑impact or heavy eccentric loading for 2‑3 days; continue gentle daily activities as tolerated.  
3. Encourage active recovery: light walking, low‑intensity cycling, and gentle stretching of the quadriceps and hamstrings.  
4. Use over‑the‑counter NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen 400 mg q6‑8 h) or acetaminophen for pain if needed, provided no contraindications.  
5. Apply local heat (warm compress or warm shower) before activity and consider cold packs after activity if soreness is pronounced.  
6. Maintain adequate hydration and balanced nutrition, including protein intake to support muscle repair.  
7. Educate on gradual progression: increase exercise volume/intensity by no more than 10 % per week and incorporate proper warm‑up and cool‑down routines.  
8. Instruct to seek medical evaluation if pain becomes severe, persistent beyond 5‑7 days, is associated with swelling, dark urine, fever, or functional limitation.  

Notes: None

- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.

Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.

Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. - If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.

Vignette:
A 26-year-old female marathon runner presents with a 3-week history of gradually worsening pain over the dorsum of her right foot, specifically in the region of the third metatarsal. The pain initially occurred only during long runs but now is present with walking and at rest. She significantly increased her training mileage six weeks ago in preparation for an upcoming marathon. She has a history of irregular menstrual periods and follows a restrictive diet. On examination, there is focal tenderness and mild soft-tissue swelling over the mid-shaft of the third metatarsal. Pain is elicited with the tuning fork test and with axial loading of the third toe. She has a BMI of 19. Foot radiographs obtained at another facility one week ago were normal.
winner_protocol:
Age: 26  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Gradually worsening dorsal right foot pain localized to the third metatarsal, initially during long runs and now present with walking and at rest.  

Analysis: The patient is a high‑volume runner who recently increased mileage, has focal tenderness, mild swelling, a positive tuning‑fork (bone) test, and pain with axial loading of the third toe. These findings are classic for a metatarsal stress fracture, which often remains radiographically occult in early stages. The irregular menstrual cycles and restrictive diet raise concern for the female athlete triad (low energy availability, menstrual dysfunction, decreased bone mineral density), further predisposing to stress injuries. Main differentials to consider are metatarsalgia, extensor tendonitis, Morton's neuroma, and early osteomyelitis, but the combination of activity increase, localized bone pain, and risk factors makes a stress fracture the most likely diagnosis.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: MRI of the right foot (or bone scintigraphy) to confirm stress fracture; DEXA scan to assess bone mineral density given menstrual irregularities and restrictive diet.  

Conclusion: Probable third metatarsal stress fracture secondary to recent training surge and possible low bone density from the female athlete triad.  

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  

Subclinical specialization: Orthopedics  

Recommendations:  
1. **Imaging:** Obtain MRI of the right foot (or a three‑phase bone scan) within the next few days to confirm the stress fracture.  
2. **Activity modification:** Immediately cease high‑impact running; use a stiff‑soled shoe or a controlled ankle‑motion (CAM) walking boot for 4–6 weeks to off‑load the third metatarsal.  
3. **Pain control:** NSAIDs as needed, avoiding excessive dosing that may impair bone healing.  
4. **Nutrition & menstrual health:** Refer to a sports dietitian and a gynecologist/endocrinologist for evaluation of energy availability, calcium/vitamin D intake, and menstrual irregularities; consider supplementation (calcium 1000 mg/day, vitamin D 800–1000 IU/day).  
5. **Bone health assessment:** Schedule a DEXA scan to evaluate for low bone mineral density; if osteopenia/osteoporosis is identified, initiate appropriate management.  
6. **Rehabilitation:** After imaging confirmation and initial immobilization, begin a graduated return‑to‑run program under supervision of a sports medicine/physical therapy team, focusing on strength, flexibility, and gradual mileage increase.  
7. **Follow‑up:** Re‑evaluate clinically in 2–3 weeks; repeat imaging if symptoms persist or worsen.  

Notes: None.

Vignette:
A 6-month-old male infant is brought in by his mother due to small red bumps on his neck and chest noticed today. The family lives in a hot climate and the air conditioning has been broken for the past 3 days. The infant has been dressed in multiple layers. He is feeding well, has normal wet diapers, and has no fever. On examination, temperature is 37.1°C. There are numerous small erythematous papules and tiny vesicles clustered on the neck, upper chest, and skin folds. The infant is alert, active, and well-hydrated.
winner_protocol:
Age: 6 months  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Small red bumps (erythematous papules and tiny vesicles) on neck and chest.  
Analysis: The infant presents with numerous small erythematous papules and vesicles localized to the neck, upper chest, and skin folds. He is afebrile, well‑hydrated, feeding normally, and otherwise healthy. The recent environmental heat exposure (broken air‑conditioning, multiple clothing layers) is a classic precipitant of miliaria (heat rash). The distribution in skin folds and the appearance of papules/vesicles strongly support miliaria rubra. Differential considerations such as viral exanthem, bacterial infection, allergic dermatitis, or infantile eczema are less likely given the acute onset, lack of systemic symptoms, and clear heat‑related trigger.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  
Conclusion: The findings are most consistent with heat rash (miliaria rubra) secondary to overheating.  
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate  
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology  
Recommendations:  
1. Immediately move the infant to a cooler environment (air‑conditioned room or fan).  
2. Remove excess clothing; dress the infant in lightweight, breathable fabrics.  
3. Keep the affected skin dry; gently pat skin dry after bathing, avoid rubbing.  
4. Apply a mild, fragrance‑free barrier ointment (e.g., zinc oxide or petroleum jelly) to reduce friction and moisture.  
5. Use cool (not cold) compresses on affected areas for symptom relief.  
6. Monitor for signs of secondary infection (increased redness, swelling, pus, fever). If any of these develop, seek medical evaluation.  
7. Educate caregivers on preventing recurrence: maintain a comfortable ambient temperature, limit layers, and ensure regular diaper and skin‑fold changes to keep skin dry.  
Notes: None

criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.

criterion:

First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.

Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.

Vignette:
A 24-yr-old man comes to the emergency department (ED) because of sudden onset of
shortness of breath and back pain. Yesterday, the patient was completing a 2-mile run, which
he does 2 times/wk, when he suddenly experienced shortness of breath and sharp pain in his
spine and on the right side of his back. The pain is constant, mild, and nonradiating and does
not worsen during movement. His shortness of breath continued throughout the night and
caused difficulty sleeping. The shortness of breath is worse this morning, prompting him to
come to the ED.

Review of Systems:
General: Has been feeling well and doing his normal activities until symptoms began yesterday.
No fever, chills, or malaise.

Skin: Noncontributory

HEENT: Reports frequent runny nose.

Pulmonary: Shortness of breath that is present at rest and worsens during exertion. No cough or
wheezing.

Cardiovascular: No chest pain or palpitations.

Gastrointestinal: Noncontributory

Genitourinary: Noncontributory

Musculoskeletal:Back pain as per his history of present illness.

Neurologic: No numbness or weakness of extremities.

Psychiatric: Noncontributory

Past Medical History:
Medical history: None; sees a physician regularly for routine physicals. No history of similar
illness or symptoms.

Surgical history: None

Medications: None

Allergies: None

Family history: Both parents are alive; father has hypertension; mother is well. Maternal
grandfather may have died of lung cancer. No known coronary artery disease in family.

Social history: Lives with his parents and works full-time in a grocery store; does occasional light
lifting without difficulty. Smokes 7 to 10 cigarettes/day, which is decreased from 1 pack/day.
Drinks alcohol once/wk to once/mo. Used marijuana in his teens.

Physical Examination:
General appearance: Well-appearing, normal body habitus, and in no distress.

Vital signs:
Temperature: 36.2° C
Pulse: 79 beats/min
Respirations: 18/min
BP: 122/72 mm Hg

Pulse oximetry: 94% on room air

Skin: No cyanosis, diaphoresis, rash, or other lesions.

HEENT: Anicteric sclerae, pupils equally round and reactive to light. Oropharynx clear.

Pulmonary: Normal respiratory effort. Decreased breath sounds on the right side.

Cardiovascular: Normal rate, regular rhythm. No murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Jugular venous
pressure is not elevated. Pulses normal and symmetric in upper and lower extremities.

Gastrointestinal: Soft, nontender, nondistended abdomen; normal bowel sounds.

Genitourinary: Not assessed

Musculoskeletal: Chest, back, and spine nontender; no palpable crepitance. Extremities appear
normal; no leg swelling, erythema, or tenderness.

Neurologic: Upper and lower extremities have normal, symmetric strength, sensation, and deep
tendon reflexes in upper and lower extremities. Gait normal.

Mental status: Appropriate. Alert and oriented.

Age: 24  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Sudden onset shortness of breath with right‑sided back pain after running.  
Analysis: The patient is a young, otherwise healthy male smoker who developed acute dyspnea at rest with unilateral decreased breath sounds on the right. These findings are classic for a primary spontaneous pneumothorax (PSP). The back pain is likely pleuritic in nature. Absence of fever, cough, wheeze, chest pain, or cardiovascular instability makes infectious or cardiac causes less likely. Differential considerations include:  
- Primary spontaneous pneumothorax (most likely)  
- Pulmonary embolism (less likely: no pleuritic chest pain, normal vitals, no risk factors)  
- Musculoskeletal strain (unlikely given decreased breath sounds)  
- Pneumonia or pleuritis (no fever, cough, infiltrates expected)  
Thus, the working diagnosis is PSP pending imaging confirmation.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Chest radiograph (PA and lateral) of the thorax; bedside lung ultrasound can be used for rapid confirmation. If the X‑ray is equivocal or a large pneumothorax is suspected, consider CT chest.  
Conclusion: The presentation is most consistent with a primary spontaneous pneumothorax on the right side.  
Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Pulmonology  
Recommendations:  
1. Place the patient on supplemental oxygen (≥2 L/min via nasal cannula) while awaiting imaging.  
2. Obtain immediate chest X‑ray (PA view) to confirm pneumothorax size and assess for tension physiology.  
3. If bedside ultrasound is available, perform a rapid lung scan (look for absent lung sliding, lung point).  
4. If a large or tension pneumothorax is identified, initiate emergent needle decompression (right 2nd intercostal space, mid‑clavicular line) followed by chest tube thoracostomy per institutional protocol.  
5. For a small, stable pneumothorax, consider observation with supplemental O₂, repeat imaging in 4–6 hours, and discharge with outpatient follow‑up if stable.  
6. Consult thoracic surgery or pulmonology early for definitive management decisions.  
7. Counsel the patient on smoking cessation and avoidance of activities that increase intrathoracic pressure until fully resolved.  
Notes: None

Diagnosis10: Toxic effect: Organophosphate and carbamate insecticides
Vignette: A 45-year-old male farmer is brought in by coworkers after collapsing in the field approximately 30 minutes after spraying crops with an organophosphate insecticide without adequate protective equipment. Coworkers report he initially complained of blurred vision and a headache, then developed profuse sweating, drooling, and vomiting before becoming unresponsive. criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.

criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.

criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.

Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.

- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.

Vignette:
A 45-year-old male farmer is brought in by coworkers after collapsing in the field approximately 30 minutes after spraying crops with an organophosphate insecticide without adequate protective equipment. Coworkers report he initially complained of blurred vision and a headache, then developed profuse sweating, drooling, and vomiting before becoming unresponsive. On examination, his clothes are damp with sweat and have a garlic-like odor. He is obtunded with labored breathing. Vital signs: T 37.0C, HR 48 (bradycardia), RR 12 (shallow, with audible secretions), BP 88/52, SpO2 84% on room air. Pupils are constricted bilaterally at 1 mm (miosis) and non-reactive. There are copious oral and bronchial secretions. Diffuse wheezing and crackles are auscultated. Fasciculations are visible in the extremities and face. He is incontinent of urine and stool. The patient is decontaminated, intubated for airway protection, and atropine 2 mg IV is administered with repeat dosing until secretions dry, followed by pralidoxime infusion.
winner_protocol:
Age: 45  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Collapse with cholinergic crisis after organophosphate pesticide exposure  

Analysis: The patient presents with classic signs of acute organophosphate poisoning—blurred vision, headache, profuse sweating, drooling, vomiting, miosis, bradycardia, hypotension, bronchorrhea, wheezing, crackles, fasciculations, and loss of bladder/bowel control. The timing (≈30 min after spraying without protection) and the garlic‑like odor on clothing further support exposure to an organophosphate insecticide. The pathophysiology is irreversible inhibition of acetylcholinesterase, leading to accumulation of acetylcholine at muscarinic and nicotinic receptors (DUMBELS). Differential considerations include other cholinergic toxidromes (carbamate poisoning, nerve agents), opioid overdose (but would have pinpoint pupils without secretions), anaphylaxis (would have urticaria, not fasciculations), and severe hypoxia. The most likely diagnosis is acute organophosphate poisoning with impending respiratory failure.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests:  
- Arterial blood gas (ABG) with lactate  
- Serum/plasma cholinesterase level (baseline and trend)  
- Electrocardiogram (ECG)  
- Chest radiograph (CXR)  
- Continuous pulse oximetry and capnography  
- Basic metabolic panel, CBC  

Conclusion: Acute organophosphate poisoning causing a severe cholinergic crisis with respiratory compromise; requires aggressive anticholinergic (atropine) and oxime (pralidoxime) therapy, airway protection, and intensive supportive care.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care  

Subclinical specialization: Emergency  

Recommendations:  
1. **Airway & Breathing** – Maintain mechanical ventilation; ensure end‑tidal CO₂ monitoring.  
2. **Atropine** – Continue IV boluses (1–2 mg every 5 min) until bronchial secretions are dry and heart rate >80 bpm; then start a continuous infusion (0.05–0.1 mg/kg/hr) with titration.  
3. **Pralidoxime** – Give a loading dose of 30 mg/kg IV over 30 min, followed by an infusion of 8–10 mg/kg/hr for 24–48 h (adjust for renal function).  
4. **Seizure prophylaxis** – Administer a benzodiazepine (e.g., diazepam 5 mg IV) if seizures or severe muscle fasciculations occur.  
5. **Hemodynamic support** – Administer isotonic crystalloid bolus; consider norepinephrine if MAP remains <65 mmHg despite fluids.  
6. **Decontamination** – Ensure thorough skin decontamination (soap and water) and removal of contaminated clothing; prevent secondary exposure to staff.  
7. **Laboratory monitoring** – Obtain ABG, electrolytes, glucose, CBC, and cholinesterase levels; repeat cholinesterase to gauge recovery.  
8. **Adjunctive care** – Consider activated charcoal if ingestion is suspected and airway is protected (already intubated).  
9. **ICU admission** – Transfer to a monitored ICU setting for continued ventilation, titration of antidotes, and observation for delayed neurotoxicity.  
10. **Education & Prevention** – Counsel patient on proper PPE and safe pesticide handling to prevent recurrence.  

Notes: None

criterion:
Step 1: Does the protocol contain a medically incorrect statement, that is, one that does not align with current medical consensus or applicable clinical guidelines? Consider the interpretation of the history, examination findings and any test results that the case provides, the diagnostic conclusion, and the selection, dose, route, frequency, duration, contraindications and interactions of any recommended treatment. Judge recommendations in the context of the patient-specific information provided in the case, including relevant age, pregnancy status, comorbidities, organ function, allergies and concurrent medications when these are stated. If yes, fail.
Step 2: Does the protocol recommend an investigation, medication or intervention that is not clinically indicated for this case, for example imaging that would not change management, antibiotics without an indication, or treatment beyond what the presentation supports? If yes, fail.
Only errors that could change management or mislead the reader count against these steps. A wording imprecision that no clinician would act on differently is not by itself a failure.
Judge only the medical correctness of the content that is present. Whether required content is missing is graded elsewhere, and so is whether the stated conclusion is properly supported by the case.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:completeness']
criterion:
The protocol must fill every field of the required schema, namely Age, Sex, Complaint, Analysis, Required diagnostic equipment/tests, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Recommendations and Notes, with case-specific content, and the content of each field must be sufficient for another clinician to act on without returning to the case text.
The value "Not specified" is a complete answer for Age or Sex when the case does not state them. The value "None" is a complete answer for Required diagnostic equipment/tests when no further workup is needed to manage the case, and for Notes when there is no essential caveat. Using these values in those situations is not a failure.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a field is absent, left empty, or filled with a placeholder or a restatement of the field label, or contains only generic content that could apply to almost any case
- the Analysis field does not name the findings from the case that drive the assessment,
- the Recommendations field does not state concrete next steps, that is, what is to be done and where or in what timeframe,
- the case warrants follow-up or safety-netting, meaning instructions on what should prompt the patient to seek care again, and no such instruction appears anywhere in the protocol,
- "None" is used for a field that this case clearly requires, for example no further workup is proposed although the conclusion is not yet established.
Do not fail a field merely because information that properly belongs in another field is not duplicated there.
Judge only whether the required content is present. The medical correctness of the content that is present is graded elsewhere, and so is the wording in which expectations are conveyed to the patient.

tags: ['axis:reasoning']
criterion:
Step 1:Does the Analysis field make the reasoning from the case findings to the Conclusion traceable?  The key findings that actually support the stated conclusion must be named, and the Analysis must make clear why they support that conclusion rather than merely listing case facts or restating the diagnosis. Where the protocol raises competing explanations it must say what makes the chosen one more likely rather than leaving them side by side. A conclusion presented with no supporting rationale drawn from the case fails this step even if the conclusion itself is correct. If not, fail.
Step 2: Are the fields of the protocol mutually consistent? The Complaint, Analysis, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Required diagnostic equipment/tests and Recommendations must not contradict one another. Examples of contradictions: an Emergency type of self-care alongside a recommendation to attend the emergency department, a Conclusion naming one condition while the Recommendations manage another, a Subclinical specialization that does not correspond to the condition concluded, or a test listed as required whose result the Analysis already assumes. If they contradict, fail.
A conditional assessment, that is, one that lays out more than one scenario, is not a failure of this criterion, provided the conditions themselves follow from the case.
Judge only the logical connection between the case findings and the stated conclusion and the internal consistency of the protocol
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:urgency']
criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:uncertainty']
criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.
